name: Potassium nitrate desensitising toothpaste

lead: This is a toothpaste containing potassium nitrate, made to reduce dentine hypersensitivity, the sharp pain from exposed dentine in response to cold, heat or touch. Whitening users use it because tooth sensitivity is the most common side effect of peroxide bleaching.

It helps whitening indirectly: calmer teeth make it easier to complete a course and reach a brighter smile. Cochrane reviews have assessed potassium toothpastes for dentine hypersensitivity, and laboratory work has examined whether potassium nitrate blocks dentinal tubules. Trials aimed specifically at whitening sensitivity were not found.

paras: Used as an ordinary toothpaste around peroxide bleaching. Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article says potassium nitrate and sodium fluoride toothpastes can ease whitening sensitivity.
It is an over-the-counter product with no specific risks noted in the sources. There is no evidence it permanently prevents whitening sensitivity, so it eases rather than eliminates it.

chain: Whiter teeth over a full course
angle.text: Calming dentine sensitivity makes it easier to keep up a peroxide whitening course, which leads to a whiter smile at the end. It has been studied for dentine pain in general, not for whitening outcomes specifically.

lead: Potassium nitrate desensitising toothpaste is a toothpaste containing potassium nitrate, a compound used to reduce dentine hypersensitivity, the sharp pain from exposed dentine in response to cold, heat or touch.[1][2] In whitening communities it is mentioned as a product used around peroxide bleaching, because tooth sensitivity is the most common side effect of whitening.[3]

Cochrane reviews have assessed potassium-containing toothpastes for dentine hypersensitivity.[1][2] Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article states that potassium nitrate and sodium fluoride toothpastes can ease whitening sensitivity, though there is no evidence they permanently prevent it.[3]

paras: The main purpose of potassium toothpastes is treating dentine hypersensitivity; a survey of US practice-based network dentists found that almost all used more than one method to manage it.[4][5] Laboratory studies have also tested toothpastes applied before 35 percent hydrogen peroxide in-office bleaching, to see whether they change whitening effectiveness and enamel properties or limit mineral loss.[6][7]
Studies have compared how different desensitising toothpastes affect dentine and how potassium nitrate in varied forms occludes dentinal tubules in vitro.[8][9]

Cochrane reviews published in 2001 and 2006 assessed potassium nitrate and other potassium-containing toothpastes against control toothpastes for reducing dentine hypersensitivity.[1][2] A clinical trial has evaluated a potassium nitrate mouthwash and toothpaste for dentinal hypersensitivity, and a 2025 real-world study examined oral-health-related quality of life with anti-sensitivity toothpaste.[10][11] No studies found that test the toothpaste specifically for sensitivity caused by cosmetic whitening in the sources reviewed, apart from the in vitro bleaching work above.[6][7]
Wikipedia says home bleaching causes less sensitivity than in-office treatment, and that potassium nitrate and fluoride toothpastes can ease it without evidence that they prevent it permanently.[3]
